title: Online Proportional Apportionment
problem:
Let n,T∈ℕ, and for each t∈[T] let v^t=(v_1^t,…,v_n^t)∈[0,1)^n satisfy\nH^t:=∑_{i=1}^n v_i^t ∈ ℤ_{≥0}.\nFor i∈[n] and t∈[T], define the cumulative shares\nV_i^t:=∑_{k=1}^t v_i^k.
\nProve that there exists a probability distribution on tables a=(a_i^t)_{i∈[n],\,t∈[T]}∈{0,1}^{n×T} such that, with probability 1,

• ∑_{i=1}^n a_i^t = H^t for every t∈[T],
• a_i^t=0 whenever v_i^t=0,
• for every i∈[n] and t∈[T], one has ∑_{k=1}^t a_i^k ∈ {⌊V_i^t⌋,⌈V_i^t⌉},
\nand such that the marginals satisfy\n𝔼[a_i^t]=v_i^t  for all i∈[n], t∈[T].
\nEquivalently: every instance admits a randomized offline allocation that is ex-ante proportional and satisfies global quota at every prefix.
\nYou may invoke, without proof, any standard integrality theorem from polyhedral combinatorics (for example, for network-flow or circulation polytopes with integer lower and upper bounds), provided you justify why it applies.

explorations.label: 1a
explorations.direction: Try a synchronized rounding scheme driven by one agent-specific random shift: draw each \(\theta_i\) independently from \([0,1]\), use it to decide when to increment \(a_i^t\), and then ask whether the joint budget constraints can be enforced by a second, very limited tie-breaking vector (for example, a two-level offset or a vector reservoir that is updated as a whole). The idea is to separate the cumulative per-agent condition into a clean local rounding rule, then test whether the only global issue is a single extra degree of freedom that can be absorbed incrementally over time.
explorations.found:
The step first introduces an **independent agent-shift scheme** as a candidate construction: for each agent \(i\), draw \(\theta_i\sim\text{Uniform}[0,1]\) and define
\[
A_i^t = \big\lfloor V_i^t + \theta_i \big\rfloor,\qquad a_i^t = A_i^t - A_i^{t-1},\quad A_i^0=0.
\]
This immediately satisfies:
- **Cumulative condition**: \(A_i^t\in\{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\);
- **Marginals**: \(\mathbb{E}[a_i^t]=v_i^t\);
- **Feasibility**: \(a_i^t=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\) (since no increment when \(v_i^t=0\)).

The only missing global condition is \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^t = H^t\) for every \(t\).

The step then rewrites the problem in terms of a fractional‑part excess indicator. Set
\[
A_i^t = \lfloor V_i^t\rfloor + \delta_i^t,\qquad \delta_i^t\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Summing over \(i\) gives
\[
\sum_i A_i^t = \sum_i \lfloor V_i^t\rfloor + \sum_i \delta_i^t = \sum_i V_i^t = \text{(integer)}.
\]
Since \(\sum_i V_i^t = \sum_{k=1}^t H^k\) is integer, the \(\delta_i^t\) must satisfy the **global budget condition**
\[
\sum_i \delta_i^t = S_t := \sum_i \{V_i^t\},
\]
where \(S_t\) is an integer equal to the total fractional part of the cumulative shares.

The transition rules for \(\delta_i^t\) are derived from the fact that when the floor of \(V_i^t\) increments (i.e., \(\ell_i^t = 1\)), the indicator can only decrease; when it does not (\(\ell_i^t = 0\)), its value can only stay the same or increase. Explicitly:
- If \(\ell_i^t = 0\) (V_i^t and V_i^{t-1} lie in the same integer interval), then \(\delta_i^t \ge \delta_i^{t-1}\);
- If \(\ell_i^t = 1\) (floor increment occurs), then \(\delta_i^t \le \delta_i^{t-1}\).

The independent shift scheme already produces a valid process \(\delta_i^t\) that respects these rules, but its sum \(\sum_i\delta_i^t\) is random and equals \(S_t\) only with probability less than 1 in general.

Several strategies to enforce the exact sum condition are examined:
1. **Global offset \(\rho\) added to all thresholds**: define \(\tilde \delta_i^t = \lfloor V_i^t + \theta_i + \rho\rfloor - \lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\) with \(\rho\sim\text{Uniform}[0,1]\). This preserves marginals but does not force the sum to equal \(S_t\); the sum still fluctuates around \(S_t\).
2. **Per-time global offset \(\rho_t\)**: using separate \(\rho_t\) per time step preserves marginals but breaks the transition constraints over time (the monotonicity condition may be violated).
3. **Post-processing flips**: after drawing the independent shifts, attempt to flip some \(\delta_i^t\) (0↔1) to correct the sum while keeping marginals unbiased. Simple “flip only zeros to ones” fails when a total decrease is needed; any flip rule that modifies the unconditional probabilities without calibration violates marginals.

Thus the problem is **reduced** to a concrete coupling: construct a joint distribution over binary vectors \(\delta_i^t\) such that for each \(i,t\):
- \(\delta_i^t\in\{0,1\}\) and the monotonicity dictated by \(\ell_i^t\) holds,
- \(P(\delta_i^t=1)=\{V_i^t\}\),
- \(\sum_i \delta_i^t = S_t\) almost surely for all \(t\).

The independent shift scheme provides a candidate distribution (the product of independent Bernoulli variables with the correct marginals), but the global constraints require coupling across agents. The step does not resolve this coupling but isolates it as the core difficulty. A plausible next direction inside this approach would be to design a “global reservoir” algorithm or invoke an integrality theorem (as permitted by the problem statement) to construct the desired coupling.
explorations.rationale: This step was taken to test a natural randomized construction (independent agent-shift rounding) against the constraints of the problem. It identified that the per‑agent conditions (cumulative rounding, marginals, zero allocation when share is zero) are satisfiable by a simple scheme, leaving the global prefix budget condition as the only obstacle. By reformulating the problem in terms of the indicator \(\delta_i^t\) and its global sum condition \(\sum_i \delta_i^t = S_t\), the step distilled the difficulty into a well‑defined coupling problem. This reduction clarifies what any successful construction must achieve and provides a concrete subproblem that can be attacked with combinatorial methods, integrality theorems, or further randomized tie‑breaking mechanisms.
explorations.core_result: The independent agent-shift construction (\(a_i^t = \lfloor V_i^t+\theta_i\rfloor - \lfloor V_i^{t-1}+\theta_i\rfloor\) with \(\theta_i\sim\text{Uniform}[0,1]\)) satisfies all per‑agent conditions except the global budget constraint \(\sum_i a_i^t = H^t\). The missing condition is equivalent to requiring that for the indicator \(\delta_i^t = \mathbf{1}[V_i^t\text{ triggers a floor crossing}]\) (or equivalently \(\delta_i^t = \lfloor V_i^t+\theta_i\rfloor - \lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\)), we have \(\sum_i \delta_i^t = S_t\) almost surely, where \(S_t = \sum_i \{V_i^t\}\) is an integer. The independent scheme yields \(\delta_i^t\) with \(P(\delta_i^t=1)=\{V_i^t\}\) and respects the monotonicity (\(\delta_i^t\ge\delta_i^{t-1}\) when \(\ell_i^t=0\), \(\delta_i^t\le\delta_i^{t-1}\) when \(\ell_i^t=1\)) but the sum is not guaranteed. The problem reduces to constructing a joint distribution over binary vectors \(\delta_i^t\) satisfying these three constraints simultaneously. Several attempted tie‑breaking strategies (global offset, per‑time offset, post‑processing flips) fail to enforce the exact sum without breaking some other condition. The existence of a valid distribution is therefore equivalent to solving this coupling problem, which remains unresolved by this step.

explorations.label: 1b
explorations.direction: Build a layered network-circulation model where each time layer \(t\) is a supernode \(S_t\) with supply \(H^t\), and each agent \(i\) is represented by a vertical chain of state nodes at time \(t\): node \((i,t,k)\) for \(k=0,1,\dots,n\) with edge \((i,t,k)\to (i,t,k+1)\) of lower bound \(\left\lfloor V_i^{t+1}-V_i^t\right\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\left\lceil V_i^{t+1}-V_i^t\right\rceil\), capacity 1. Horizontal edges from \(S_t\) to the top of each agent chain should encode \(a_i^t\). Then check whether the cumulative conditions can be expressed purely as balance equations on these states, so that integral feasibility follows by Hoffman/circulation-integrality after identifying the finite fractional structure at each time.
explorations.found:
The executed step builds a directed flow network \(G\) that encodes all constraints of the problem. The construction is as follows.

**Nodes**: For each agent \(i\in[n]\), time \(t=0,\dots,T\) and cumulative count \(k=0,\dots,n\), a node \(v_{i,t,k}\) is created (initial time \(t=0\) only uses \(k=0\) but the full grid is included for uniformity). For each time \(t=1,\dots,T\) a supply node \(S_t\) is added, and a sink node \(T\) is added.

**Edges**:
1. *Agent-chain edges*: for each \(i\), \(t=0,\dots,T-1\) and \(k=0,\dots,n-1\) there are two edges:
   - \((i,t,k)\to(i,t+1,k)\) (no increment), lower bound \(0\), upper bound \(1\).
   - \((i,t,k)\to(i,t+1,k+1)\) (increment), lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^{t+1}-V_i^t\rfloor = 0\) (since \(V_i^{t+1}-V_i^t = v_i^{t+1}\in[0,1)\)), upper bound \(\lceil V_i^{t+1}-V_i^t\rceil\) which equals \(1\) if \(v_i^{t+1}>0\) and \(0\) otherwise – so the edge effectively exists only when \(v_i^{t+1}>0\).
2. *Time-supply edges*: for each time \(t=1,\dots,T\) and each \(i,k\) there is an edge \(S_t\to v_{i,t-1,k}\) with capacity \(1\) (upper bound). These edges inject the supply at time \(t\) into the agent-state nodes of the previous time step.
3. *Sink edges*: for each agent \(i\) and \(k=0,\dots,n\) there is an edge \(v_{i,T,k}\to T\) with infinite capacity (or at least \(n\)).

**Supplies and demands**: Each \(S_t\) has supply \(H^t\) (so outflow from \(S_t\) must sum to \(H^t\)). The sink \(T\) has demand \(\sum_{t=1}^T H^t\). All other nodes have net zero flow.

**Interpretation as an allocation**: A unit of flow starting at \(S_t\), passing through an agent-chain edge, and ending at a node \(v_{i,T,k}\) that then goes to \(T\) encodes a path \((i,t-1,k)\to(i,t,k+1)\to\cdots\). The flow on the increment edges represents the amount of allocation to agent \(i\) at time \(t\) given that the cumulative before time \(t\) was \(k\). Capacity \(1\) on \(S_t\to v_{i,t-1,k}\) ensures at most one unit is allocated to the same agent at the same time step, and the absence of an increment edge when \(v_i^{t+1}=0\) enforces \(a_i^t=0\) for zero fractional shares.

**Feasibility of the fractional point**: The step shows that the fractional point \(a_i^t = v_i^t\) (for all \(i,t\)) corresponds to a feasible flow in this network. The construction uses a coupling that yields a joint distribution of cumulative counts \((C_i^t)\) whose marginals are \(\{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\) with the right expectations. This distribution defines a flow where for each time \(t\) the outflow from \(S_t\) is exactly \(H^t\), and the cumulative inflow into the chain up to time \(t\) satisfies the lower/upper bounds \(\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\) and \(\lceil V_i^t\rceil\). All capacity constraints are respected because the lower/upper bounds on the increment edges are exactly the fractional increments.

**Integrality argument**: The node-arc incidence matrix of a directed graph is totally unimodular; all supplies (\(H^t\)) and demands are integers; all edge lower/upper bounds are integers (0 or 1). Hence the feasible region for flows is an integral polytope — its vertices are integral. The feasible fractional flow corresponds to an interior point, so it can be expressed as a convex combination of integral extreme points. Each integral flow corresponds to a deterministic allocation \(a_i^t\in\{0,1\}\) that satisfies \(\sum_i a_i^t = H^t\), \(a_i^t=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^k \in \{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\). Taking the distribution that assigns probability proportional to the weights in the convex combination yields a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{n\times T}\) with marginals \(\mathbb{E}[a_i^t]=v_i^t\) and all constraints satisfied almost surely. The step concludes that the direction is fully successful — no obstruction was encountered.
explorations.rationale: This step was taken to transform the original fractional allocation problem into a flow network whose integral extreme points automatically satisfy the structural constraints. By constructing an explicit network that embeds the global quota, per-time symmetry, and cumulative floor/ceil conditions, and then applying the integrality of network flow polytopes (total unimodularity), the existence of a randomized offline allocation follows directly from the feasibility of the fractional point. The construction provides a concrete combinatorial object that can be used for further analysis or algorithmic manipulation.

explorations.label: 1c
explorations.direction: Recast the whole problem as a single-source circulation on neighbor sets \(N_t=\{i: v_i^t>0\}\). Put one supply \(H^t\) at time \(t\), capacity \(1\) on each \(t\!\to\!i\) arc, and auxiliary copy/cumulative nodes whose lower/upper bounds encode the interval \([\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\) for the prefix through \(t\). The next thing to try is to prove that, if a fractional circulation on these aggregated variables satisfies the total demands, then it can be split into unit disjoint paths that become the desired allocation matrix \(a_i^t\).
explorations.found:
The step models the allocation problem as a single‑source, single‑sink directed flow network.
**Nodes:** a source \(S\), a sink \(D\), time nodes \(T_t\) for \(t=1,\dots,T\), and item‑cumulative nodes \(P_{i,t}\) for \(i=1,\dots,n\) and \(t=1,\dots,T\) (\(P_{i,0}\) is considered a source with zero flow).  
**Arcs and their bounds:**  

1. \(S\to T_t\): lower bound = upper bound = \(H^t\) (forces exactly \(H^t\) units to enter each time node).  
2. For each \(i\) with \(v_i^t>0\): \(T_t\to P_{i,t}\) with capacity 1 (lower bound 0, upper bound 1). If \(v_i^t=0\) the arc is omitted, forcing \(a_i^t=0\) in any feasible flow.  
3. For each \(i\) and \(t=1,\dots,T-1\): \(P_{i,t}\to P_{i,t+1}\) with lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^t\rceil\) — this edge carries the cumulative allocation up to time \(t\).  
4. For each \(i\): \(P_{i,T}\to D\) with lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^T\rceil\).  

**Flow conservation:**  

- At \(T_t\): inflow from \(S\) equals total outflow to all \(P_{i,t}\) (so the outflow from \(T_t\) is \(H^t\)).  
- At \(P_{i,t}\) for \(1\le t\le T-1\): inflow from \(T_t\) plus inflow from \(P_{i,t-1}\) equals outflow to \(P_{i,t+1}\).  
- At \(P_{i,T}\): inflow from \(T_T\) plus inflow from \(P_{i,T-1}\) equals outflow to \(D\).  

**Fractional solution:**  
Set  

\[
x_{i,t}=v_i^t \quad\text{(flow on }T_t\to P_{i,t}\text{)},\qquad
y_{i,t}=V_i^t \quad\text{(flow on }P_{i,t}\to P_{i,t+1}\text{ for }t=1,\dots,T-1),\qquad
d_{i,T}=V_i^T\quad\text{(flow on }P_{i,T}\to D\text{)}.
\]

- \(\sum_i v_i^t = H^t\) ensures that all \(S\to T_t\) arcs are saturated.  
- For each \(i,t\) with \(v_i^t>0\), \(0\le v_i^t\le 1\) respects the capacity 1 on \(T_t\to P_{i,t}\).  
- For each \(i,t\), \(V_i^t\in[\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\) respects the lower/upper bounds on the cumulative arcs.  
- Conservation at \(P_{i,t}\) holds because  
  \[
  x_{i,t}+V_i^{t-1}=V_i^t,\qquad V_i^{T-1}+x_{i,T}=V_i^T.
  \]

Thus the fractional vector is a feasible flow in this network when all capacities and bounds are interpreted as intervals. The constraint matrix is a node‑arc incidence matrix of a directed graph (each arc contributes one \(+1\) and one \(-1\) in the equations), which is **totally unimodular** (TU). By a standard integrality result for network flows (Hoffman’s circulation theorem), the feasible region defined by these TU constraints, integer lower/upper bounds, and integer supplies/demands is an **integral polytope**: every extreme point is integral. Because the fractional flow lies inside this polytope, it can be expressed as a convex combination of integer extreme‑point flows.  

Each integer extreme point corresponds to a deterministic table \(a_i^t\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying:  

- \(\sum_i a_i^t = H^t\) (exactly \(H^t\) units at each time),  
- \(a_i^t=0\) when \(v_i^t=0\),  
- \(\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^k \in [\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\).  

Taking the convex combination yields a probability distribution over such tables with marginals \(\mathbb{E}[a_i^t]=v_i^t\). This is precisely the desired randomized offline allocation.
explorations.rationale: This step reduces the combinatorial allocation problem to a flow network that naturally encodes the quota and prefix constraints through arc capacities and flow conservation. The integrality of the network flow polytope (a consequence of total unimodularity) guarantees that the given fractional solution can be decomposed into a convex combination of integral allocations, directly proving existence of the required distribution. This approach provides a clean, constructive proof that avoids explicit enumeration.
explorations.core_result:
There exists a probability distribution over tables \(a=(a_i^t)\in\{0,1\}^{n\times T}\) such that with probability 1:

- \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^t = H^t\) for every \(t\in[T]\),  
- \(a_i^t=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\) for every \(i\in[n],t\in[T]\),  
- \(\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^k \in \{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\) for every \(i\in[n],t\in[T]\),  

and the marginals satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[a_i^t]=v_i^t\) for all \(i,t\). This follows by constructing the described flow network, verifying that the fractional vector \((v_i^t, V_i^t)\) is feasible, invoking total unimodularity, and applying Hoffman’s circulation theorem to obtain an integral decomposition.

The move is to eliminate or explicitly identify the surplus/drift variable so that the feasible set becomes a standard circulation polytope with integer lower and upper bounds on all boundary arcs. explorations.found: The executed step formalizes the flow network from Exploration 1c into a pure circulation polytope, applying Hoffman’s circulation integrality theorem to prove existence of the required distribution. The construction adds one extra arc \(D \to S\) (lower bound \(0\), upper bound \(\sum_{t=1}^T H^t\)) so that every node has net zero flow, converting the source‑sink flow into a circulation. All arcs are now part of a directed graph with integer lower/upper bounds: \(S \to T_t\) forced to \(H^t\) (integer); \(T_t \to P_{i,t}\) when \(v_i^t>0\) (0 or 1); \(P_{i,t}\to P_{i,t+1}\) for \(t=1,\dots,T-1\) with bounds \([\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\) (both integers); \(P_{i,T}\to D\) with bounds \([\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor,\lceil V_i^T\rceil]\); and the dummy arc \(D\to S\) with bounds \([0,\sum_t H^t]\). The fractional data \(x_{i,t}=v_i^t\), \(y_{i,t}=V_i^t\), \(z_i=V_i^T\), \(f_{S,t}=H^t\), \(f_{D\to S}=\sum_t H^t\) is verified to satisfy all bounds and conservation equalities, thus making it a feasible circulation. Because the node‑arc incidence matrix of any directed graph is totally unimodular, and all bounds and supplies are integers, the feasible circulation polytope is an integral polytope—all vertices are integral. The fractional circulation lies inside this polytope, so it can be expressed as a convex combination of integral extreme‑point circulations. Each integral circulation corresponds to a deterministic allocation table \(a_i^t\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying: \(\sum_i a_i^t = H^t\) (from conservation at \(T_t\)), \(a_i^t=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\) (arc omitted), and \(\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^k = y_{i,t} \in \{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\). Taking the convex combination as a probability distribution yields exactly the required randomized offline allocation—the desired existence proof is achieved without encountering any obstruction.

While the earlier flow network already had a source and sink, converting it into a balanced circulation eliminates transient imbalances and aligns with the standard theorem (Hoffman’s circulation theorem) that guarantees integrality for bounded‑edge circulation polytopes with integer bounds. By verifying the integrality of extreme points and exhibiting a feasible fractional circulation (the data itself), the step closes the existence proof: the existence of a randomized allocation follows immediately without needing to construct the distribution explicitly.

Instead of relying only on the abstract integrality theorem, stress-test the statement that each unit of integral flow in the circulation model corresponds to one binary decision a_i^t \in {0,1}: inspect whether every unit can be seen as a path/cut decomposition, and separately confirm that the time-t quota, zero-share exclusion, and cumulative floor/ceil bounds are all represented by arc capacity and path conservation. explorations.found:
The step takes the flow network constructed in Explorations 1c (and similarly 1b) and inspects the mapping from an integral extreme‑point flow to a deterministic binary allocation table \(a_i^t \in \{0,1\}\). The network has source \(S\), sink \(D\), time nodes \(T_t\) for each \(t=1,\dots,T\), and agent‑cumulative nodes \(P_{i,t}\) for each \(i\in[n], t=1,\dots,T\). Arcs and their integer bounds are:

- \(S \to T_t\): lower bound = upper bound = \(H^t\).
- \(T_t \to P_{i,t}\): capacity 1 if \(v_i^t>0\); omitted if \(v_i^t=0\).
- For \(t=1,\dots,T-1\): \(P_{i,t} \to P_{i,t+1}\) with lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^t\rceil\).
- For each \(i\): \(P_{i,T} \to D\) with lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^T\rceil\).

Flow conservation is: at \(T_t\), inflow from \(S\) equals total outflow to all \(P_{i,t}\) (so exactly \(H^t\) units leave \(T_t\)); at \(P_{i,t}\) (\(1\le t\le T-1\)), inflow from \(T_t\) plus inflow from \(P_{i,t-1}\) equals outflow to \(P_{i,t+1}\); at \(P_{i,T}\), inflow from \(T_T\) plus inflow from \(P_{i,T-1}\) equals outflow to \(D\). Here \(P_{i,0}\) represents a zero inflow.

Because the network is acyclic and all bounds are integers, any feasible flow can be decomposed into a set of \(S\)-\(D\) unit paths (each carrying 1 unit). Integral extreme points correspond to such decompositions.

We prove the existence of the desired randomized allocation by constructing a flow network whose feasible region is an integral polytope and whose fractional point is the candidate allocation \((v_i^t)\). Standard integrality results then guarantee that the fractional point can be expressed as a convex combination of integral flows, each of which corresponds to a deterministic allocation table satisfying all the required conditions.

**Flow network.**  
We define a directed graph \(G\) whose nodes are:

- a source \(S\),
- a sink \(D\),
- for each time step \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\) a time node \(T_t\),
- for each agent \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) and each time step \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\) an agent‑cumulative node \(C_{i,t}\).

The arcs of \(G\) are:

1. \((S,T_t)\) for each \(t\): lower bound = upper bound = \(H^t\) (an integer);
2. \((T_t,C_{i,t})\) for each \(i,t\) with \(v_i^t>0\): lower bound \(0\), upper bound \(1\); if \(v_i^t=0\) the arc is omitted;
3. \((C_{i,t},C_{i,t+1})\) for each \(i\) and \(t=1,\dots,T-1\) with lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^t\rceil\) (both integers);
4. \((C_{i,T},D)\) for each \(i\): lower bound \(\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor\) and upper bound \(\lceil V_i^T\rceil\);
5. \((D,S)\) – an artificial return arc with lower bound \(0\) and upper bound \(\sum_{t=1}^T H^t\) (an integer).

All lower and upper bounds are integers.

**Feasible fractional flow.**  
Consider the following assignment of flows to the arcs:

- \(x_{S,T_t}=H^t\) for every \(t\);
- for each \(i,t\) with \(v_i^t>0\), \(x_{T_t,C_{i,t}}=v_i^t\);
- for each \(i\) and \(t=1,\dots,T-1\), \(x_{C_{i,t},C_{i,t+1}}=V_i^t\) (the cumulative share);
- for each \(i\), \(x_{C_{i,T},D}=V_i^T\);
- \(x_{D,S}=\sum_{t=1}^T H^t\).

We verify that every node satisfies flow conservation and that the flow respects all lower and upper bounds.

- **Node \(S\):** inflow from \(D\) is \(x_{D,S}=\sum_t H^t\); outflow is \(\sum_t x_{S,T_t}=\sum_t H^t\). Balance holds.
- **Node \(T_t\):** inflow from \(S\) is \(H^t\); outflow is \(\sum_{i: v_i^t>0} v_i^t = H^t\) because \(\sum_i v_i^t=H^t\). Balance holds.
- **Node \(C_{i,t}\) for \(t=1,\dots,T-1\):** inflow consists of \(x_{T_t,C_{i,t}}=v_i^t\) if \(v_i^t>0\) (zero otherwise) plus \(x_{C_{i,t-1},C_{i,t}}=V_i^{t-1}\). The sum is \(V_i^{t-1}+v_i^t=V_i^t\), which equals the outflow \(x_{C_{i,t},C_{i,t+1}}\). Balance holds.
- **Node \(C_{i,T}\):** inflow is \(x_{T_T,C_{i,T}}=v_i^T\) (if \(v_i^T>0\)) plus \(x_{C_{i,T-1},C_{i,T}}=V_i^{T-1}\); total is \(V_i^{T-1}+v_i^T=V_i^T\), which equals the outflow \(x_{C_{i,T},D}\). Balance holds.
- **Node \(D\):** inflow from all \(C_{i,T}\) is \(\sum_i V_i^T = \sum_{t=1}^T H^t\) (because \(V_i^T = \sum_{k=1}^T v_i^k\) and \(\sum_i V_i^T = \sum_{t=1}^T H^t\)); outflow to \(S\) is \(x_{D,S}=\sum_t H^t\). Balance holds.

All lower and upper bounds are integers and the flow on each arc lies within its bounds: \(x_{S,T_t}=H^t\) respects the equality bounds; \(x_{T_t,C_{i,t}}=v_i^t\) lies in \([0,1]\); \(x_{C_{i,t},C_{i,t+1}}=V_i^t\) lies in \([\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\); \(x_{C_{i,T},D}=V_i^T\) lies in \([\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor,\lceil V_i^T\rceil]\); and the return arc carries \(\sum_t H^t\) which is between \(0\) and \(\sum_t H^t\). Hence this assignment is a feasible circulation (all node balances are zero) in \(G\).

**Integrality.**  
The constraint matrix of the circulation system is the node–arc incidence matrix of the directed graph \(G\) (one row per node, one column per arc, with entries \(+1\) for an outgoing arc and \(-1\) for an incoming arc). For any directed graph, the node–arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular. Moreover, all lower and upper bounds on the arcs are integers, the system is homogeneous (\(Ax=0\)), and the fractional point is feasible. By Hoffman’s circulation theorem (or the standard integrality of network flow polytopes with totally unimodular matrices and integer bounds), the feasible set of circulations is an **integral polytope**: every extreme point is an integer vector. Consequently, the fractional circulation, which lies inside the polytope, can be expressed as a convex combination of integral extreme‑point circulations.

**From integrals to deterministic allocations.**  
Each integral circulation defines binary values \(a_i^t\in\{0,1\}\) as follows. Because the arc \((S,T_t)\) carries exactly \(H^t\) units, and the only outgoing arcs from \(T_t\) are the arcs \((T_t,C_{i,t})\) (each with capacity \(1\)), the number of these arcs that receive flow \(1\) must be exactly \(H^t\). Define \(a_i^t\) to be the flow on \((T_t,C_{i,t})\); then \(\sum_i a_i^t = H^t\) for every \(t\), and if \(v_i^t=0\) the arc is absent so \(a_i^t=0\).

For each agent \(i\), flow conservation at the nodes \(C_{i,t}\) yields

\[
x_{C_{i,t},C_{i,t+1}} = \sum_{j=1}^t a_i^j, \qquad (t=1,\dots,T-1),
\]

and similarly \(x_{C_{i,T},D} = \sum_{j=1}^T a_i^j\). Since the flows on these arcs are bounded by \([\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil]\), we obtain

\[
\sum_{j=1}^t a_i^j \in \{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}
\]

for all \(i\) and \(t\). Thus every integral extreme‑point circulation corresponds to a deterministic table \(a=(a_i^t)_{i\in[n],\,t\in[T]}\) that satisfies the three required conditions almost surely.

**Conclusion.**  
Take any convex combination of such integral extreme‑point circulations that represents the fractional point. The coefficients of this convex combination form a probability distribution on the tables \(a\) (since the number of extreme points may be finite). By construction, the expected flow on the arc \((T_t,C_{i,t})\) equals the fractional flow value \(v_i^t\); therefore the marginal expectations satisfy \(\mathbb{E}[a_i^t]=v_i^t\). Because the support of the distribution consists entirely of tables that meet the other constraints, we have proved the existence of a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{n\times T}\) with the desired properties. ∎

  f^*(w_i^{T-1},w_i^T)+f^*(u^T,w_i^T)=V_i^{T-1}+v_i^T=V_i^T,
  \]
  which equals outgoing flow \(f^*(w_i^T,d)\).
\nHence \(f^*\) is a feasible fractional flow.
\nBy the allowed integrality theorem, the feasible-flow polytope of this network is integral. Therefore \(f^*\) can be written as a convex combination of feasible integral flows:
\[\nf^* = \sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j f_j,
\]\nwhere each \(f_j:E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is a feasible integral flow, each \(\lambda_j>0\), and \(\sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j=1\).
\nFor each \(j\in[q]\), define a binary table \(a^{(j)}=(a_i^{t,(j)})\) by
\[\na_i^{t,(j)} := f_j(u^t,w_i^t).
\]\nWe claim that each \(a^{(j)}\) is a deterministic offline allocation satisfying global quota.
\nFirst, each \(a_i^{t,(j)}\in\{0,1\}\) because \(f_j\) is integral and the edge \((u^t,w_i^t)\) has capacity \(1\).
\nNext, we prove the row-sum condition. Since
\[\nH^t=f^*(o,u^t)=\sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j f_j(o,u^t)
\]\nand every \(f_j(o,u^t)\le c(o,u^t)=H^t\), the only way their convex combination can equal \(H^t\) is if
\[\nf_j(o,u^t)=H^t \qquad \text{for every } j.
\]\nNow flow conservation at \(u^t\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^{t,(j)}=\sum_{i=1}^n f_j(u^t,w_i^t)=f_j(o,u^t)=H^t.
\]\nSo each table allocates exactly \(H^t\) seats at time \(t\).
\nWe also need \(a_i^{t,(j)}=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\). But if \(v_i^t=0\), then
\[
0=f^*(u^t,w_i^t)=\sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j f_j(u^t,w_i^t).
\]\nAll coefficients \(\lambda_j\) are positive and all \(f_j(u^t,w_i^t)\ge 0\), so necessarily
\[\nf_j(u^t,w_i^t)=0 \qquad \text{for every } j.
\]\nHence \(a_i^{t,(j)}=0\) whenever \(v_i^t=0\).
\nIt remains to prove global quota for each \(a^{(j)}\). Fix \(j\in[q]\), \(i\in[n]\), and \(t<T\). Summing flow conservation over the vertices \(w_i^1,\dots,w_i^t\), all internal chain flows cancel, yielding
\[
\sum_{k=1}^t f_j(u^k,w_i^k)=f_j(w_i^t,w_i^{t+1}).
\]\nTherefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^{k,(j)} = f_j(w_i^t,w_i^{t+1}).
\]\nSince \(f_j\) respects the lower and upper capacities on that edge and is integral,
\[
\sum_{k=1}^t a_i^{k,(j)} \in \{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}.
\]\nFor \(t=T\), summing flow conservation over \(w_i^1,\dots,w_i^T\) gives
\[
\sum_{k=1}^T a_i^{k,(j)} = f_j(w_i^T,d),
\]\nand again integrality plus the capacity bounds imply
\[
\sum_{k=1}^T a_i^{k,(j)} \in \{\lfloor V_i^T\rfloor,\lceil V_i^T\rceil\}.
\]\nThus every \(a^{(j)}\) satisfies global quota.
\nNow define a randomized offline allocation by choosing \(a^{(j)}\) with probability \(\lambda_j\).
\nSince each \(a^{(j)}\) is a deterministic offline allocation satisfying global quota, the randomized allocation satisfies global quota almost surely.
\nFinally, we verify ex-ante proportionality. For any \(i\in[n]\) and \(t\in[T]\),
\[
\mathbb E[a_i^t]
=\sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j a_i^{t,(j)}
=\sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j f_j(u^t,w_i^t)
=f^*(u^t,w_i^t)
=v_i^t.
\]\nSo the expected seat indicator at time \(t\) for party \(i\) equals its vote share \(v_i^t\).
\nTherefore there exists a randomized offline allocation satisfying both global quota and ex-ante proportionality. This proves the claim.
